triage.name: Body Lice
triage.reason: Pruritic rash with identifiable lice/nits on exam; diagnosis reachable by history and physical, with good exposure and hygiene history.

demographics: Most common in people who cannot bathe or wash clothing regularly, especially in crowded conditions
In the United States, most often seen in people experiencing homelessness or unstable housing
Also seen in refugees, displaced persons, and victims of war or natural disasters
Occurs worldwide; no clear sex predilection

risk_factors.text: Lack of regular bathing or laundering of clothing and bedding
Crowded living conditions (shelters, encampments, refugee camps)
Sharing clothing, bedding, or towels with an infested person
Close physical contact with an infested person
Cold weather or inability to change or wash clothing for prolonged periods

comorbidities: Conditions associated with poor self-care or limited access to hygiene facilities
social_history: Shelter, encampment, or other crowded living arrangement
Limited access to showers, laundry, or clean clothing
Recent displacement, refugee, or disaster-related living situation
exposures: Contact with clothing, bedding, or towels used by a person with body lice
Close physical contact with an infested person

chief_complaints.text: I itch all over, especially under my clothes
I keep finding little bugs and eggs in the seams of my clothes
I have red bumps and scratch marks on my body

hpi.onset: Gradual; itching usually begins days to weeks after infestation, once sensitivity to louse saliva develops
hpi.duration: Weeks to months if untreated; often present for a long time before medical attention
hpi.progression: Itching starts and slowly worsens; scratching leads to sores that may become infected; with prolonged infestation, heavily bitten skin becomes thickened and discolored
hpi.location: Trunk, waist, groin, upper thighs, and areas where clothing seams and waistbands press against the skin; lice and nits are found in clothing seams rather than on the body
hpi.radiation: Usually none; itching is diffuse over clothed areas
hpi.quality: Intense, persistent itching with small red bumps and scratch marks
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; itching can be intense enough to disturb sleep
hpi.timing: Continuous, worse at night and when clothing is worn or removed
relieving: Washing clothing and bedding in hot water

associated_symptoms.text: Red bumps or rash from bites and allergic reaction
Scratch marks and sores from scratching
Thickened, darkened skin in heavily bitten areas (waist, groin, upper thighs) with long-standing infestation
Sores that become infected with bacteria or fungi
Fever, headache, or body aches suggesting a louse-borne illness such as typhus, trench fever, or relapsing fever

pertinent_negatives: Itching and nits limited to the scalp or hair
Itching and lice limited to the pubic or genital area
Burrows, tracks, or nodules between the fingers, wrists, or genitals
Recent travel to an area with sandflies or other vector-borne skin disease
Household pets with fleas or mites
Known immunocompromising condition or immunosuppressive medication

positives.text: Itching all over, worse under clothing
Red bumps or rash on the trunk, waist, and thighs
Thickened, darkened skin in bitten areas

negatives: Rash limited to the scalp or hair
Rash limited to the pubic area
Burrows or tracks in the skin
Painful nodules in the axillae or groin
argues_against: Infestation confined to the head or pubic hair
Classic scabies burrows between the fingers or on the wrists
Persistent fever with weight loss suggesting another systemic illness

positives.text: Trouble sleeping because of the itching
Feeling embarrassed or anxious about the infestation

negatives: Delusions of being infested without any evidence

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with irritability, poor sleep, and scratching rather than a clear description of itching; they may not report bugs in clothing.
missing_classic_features: Clear description of itching under clothing
Report of lice or nits in clothing seams

atypical.how_it_differs: Itching may be milder or attributed to dry skin, and skin thickening and discoloration may be more prominent after long-standing infestation.
Scratch sores are more likely to become secondarily infected, and systemic symptoms from louse-borne disease may be more severe.

general.mild: Comfortable, alert, no distress; may scratch intermittently
general.moderate: Scratching frequently, visible excoriations, mild discomfort
general.severe: Ill-appearing, restless from intense itching, extensive excoriations and possibly secondary infection
general.critical: Toxic-appearing with high fever, hypotension, or altered mental status suggesting louse-borne systemic illness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the seams, collars, cuffs, and waistbands of the patient's clothing with a magnifying lens
findings.finding: Live body lice and nits (eggs) attached to clothing fibers in the seams

findings.maneuver: Inspect the trunk, waist, groin, and upper thighs
findings.finding: Linear scratch marks and excoriations in areas covered by clothing

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin of the trunk and proximal extremities
findings.finding: Small red papules or urticarial wheals from louse bites

findings.maneuver: Observe the skin surface, especially when clothing is removed
findings.finding: A body louse crawling or feeding on the skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect excoriated areas for signs of infection
findings.finding: Pustules, crusting, or cellulitis at scratch sites

findings.maneuver: Palpate and inspect the waist, groin, and upper thighs
findings.finding: Thickened, hyperpigmented, lichenified skin in chronically bitten areas

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scalp and hair for lice and nits
findings.finding: No lice or nits on the scalp or hair shafts

findings.maneuver: Inspect the pubic hair and genital area
findings.finding: No lice or nits on pubic hair

findings.maneuver: Inspect the finger webs, wrists, and genitalia for burrows
findings.finding: No burrows, tracks, or scabetic nodules

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes

initial.why: Not routinely needed; obtained when secondary bacterial infection of excoriations is suspected (marked erythema, purulence, fever) or when a louse-borne illness is being considered
initial.only_if: secondary skin infection or louse-borne systemic illness is suspected

confirmatory.test: Microscopic examination of clothing seams for lice and nits
confirmatory.why: Finding live body lice or viable nits attached to clothing fibers confirms the diagnosis; a magnifying lens or low-power microscopy helps identify the organism

supporting.why: Performed when scabies is a serious alternative and burrows or typical distribution are present; negative result supports body lice
supporting.only_if: scabies is suspected (burrows, finger web or wrist involvement)

not_indicated.why: No routine role; body lice infestation does not cause characteristic blood count changes
Not useful for diagnosing an ectoparasitic infestation
Nonspecific and not part of the evaluation
Not needed when lice and nits are clearly identified on clothing
Not indicated; diagnosis is made by inspecting clothing and skin for the organism

decision_points: Inspect the patient's clothing seams, collars, cuffs, and waistbands with a magnifying lens before considering other causes of generalized itching
Distinguish body lice from head lice and pubic lice by where the lice and nits are found (clothing versus scalp hair versus pubic hair)
Consider scabies when burrows, finger web involvement, or a compatible rash are present
Consider louse-borne diseases (typhus, trench fever, relapsing fever) if fever, headache, or systemic symptoms accompany the infestation

differential.name: Scabies
differential.why_considered: Generalized intense itching with a papular rash and excoriations, often worse at night, in a patient with poor hygiene or crowded living conditions
differential.trigger: Burrows, tracks, or itchy nodules between the finger webs, wrists, or genitalia

history: Itching is worst at night and involves the hands, wrists, and finger webs
Similar itching in close contacts or household members
No report of bugs or nits in clothing seams
exam: Burrows or tracks in the finger webs, wrists, axillae, or genitalia
Itchy nodules on the scrotum or penis
Lice and nits absent from clothing seams
labs: Skin scraping or mineral oil preparation shows mites, eggs, or scybala

differential.name: Head lice
differential.why_considered: Lice infestation with scalp itching and visible nits, and a similar social and hygiene context

history: Itching and nits confined to the scalp and hair
Nits firmly attached to hair shafts behind the ears and at the nape
exam: Live lice or nits on scalp hair shafts
No lice or nits in clothing seams
Excoriations mainly on the scalp and neck

differential.name: Pubic lice
differential.why_considered: Lice infestation with itching in the groin and a papular rash in the pubic area

history: Itching localized to the pubic and genital area
Sexual contact with an infested partner
exam: Lice or nits attached to pubic hair
Blue-gray macules (maculae ceruleae) in the pubic area
No lice or nits in clothing seams

differential.name: Atopic dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic itchy rash with excoriations and lichenified skin in flexural or truncal areas

history: Long-standing personal or family history of eczema, asthma, or allergic rhinitis
Itching flares with soaps, heat, or stress rather than with clothing use
No bugs or nits in clothing
exam: Dry, lichenified, flexural rash
No lice, nits, or burrows
No bite papules in clothing-covered areas

differential.name: Contact dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Itchy rash in areas where clothing presses against the skin, such as the waistband and thighs

history: Onset after a new detergent, fabric, or topical product
Rash follows the shape of the contactant rather than bite patterns
No bugs or nits in clothing
exam: Well-demarcated erythema and vesiculation confined to contact areas
No lice, nits, or burrows

differential.name: Delusional parasitosis
differential.why_considered: Patient reports bugs and itching but no objective evidence of infestation

history: Fixed belief of infestation despite repeated negative examinations
Brings in samples of lint, skin, or debris as 'proof'
No response to appropriate treatment
exam: No lice, nits, or burrows on repeated careful inspection
Excoriations may be present but no bite papules

differential.name: Louse-borne relapsing fever
differential.why_considered: Body lice can transmit Borrelia recurrentis, causing fever and systemic illness in an infested patient
differential.trigger: Fever, headache, and body aches in a patient with body lice

history: Recurrent episodes of fever lasting several days separated by afebrile periods
Headache, muscle aches, and malaise
Body lice infestation with poor hygiene
exam: Fever, tachycardia, and possibly hepatosplenomegaly
Lice and nits in clothing seams

differential.name: Epidemic typhus
differential.why_considered: Body lice transmit Rickettsia prowazekii, which can cause fever, rash, and systemic illness in infested patients
differential.trigger: High fever, severe headache, and a rash in a patient with body lice

history: High fever, severe headache, and myalgias
Rash appearing several days into illness
Crowded living conditions with body lice
exam: Macular or petechial rash spreading from the trunk to the extremities
Fever and possibly hypotension
Lice and nits in clothing seams

severity.mild: Itching and a few bite papules with lice and nits limited to clothing seams; no excoriations or secondary infection
severity.moderate: Intense itching with widespread excoriations, sleep disturbance, and early skin thickening in bitten areas
severity.severe: Extensive excoriations with secondary bacterial infection, marked lichenification and hyperpigmentation, and significant distress
severity.critical: Systemic louse-borne illness (typhus, trench fever, or relapsing fever) with high fever, hypotension, or altered mental status

red_flags.finding: High fever with headache and rash
red_flags.meaning: Possible louse-borne disease such as typhus or relapsing fever; needs urgent evaluation and treatment
Sepsis or severe systemic illness from a louse-borne infection
Severe systemic infection or another serious cause; urgent workup

red_flags.finding: Spreading erythema, purulence, or fluctuance at scratch sites
red_flags.meaning: Secondary bacterial skin infection such as cellulitis or abscess

complications.name: Secondary bacterial skin infection
clues: Increasing pain, redness, or purulence at scratch sites

complications.name: Lichenification and hyperpigmentation
clues: Thickened, darkened skin at the waist, groin, and upper thighs

complications.name: Epidemic typhus
clues: High fever, severe headache, and rash

complications.name: Trench fever
clues: Positive Bartonella quintana serology or culture

special_populations.differences: May present with irritability and poor sleep rather than a clear description of itching; inspect clothing seams carefully and treat the whole household.
Itching may be milder or attributed to dry skin; chronic skin thickening and discoloration may be more prominent.
Scratch sores are more likely to become secondarily infected, and systemic louse-borne disease may be more severe.
Treatment should avoid agents with uncertain safety; permethrin is generally preferred, and hygiene measures are the mainstay.

key_questions.question: Where do you itch the most, and is it under your clothes?
key_questions.looking_for: Itching concentrated on the trunk, waist, groin, and upper thighs, in areas covered by clothing

key_questions.question: Have you noticed tiny bugs or eggs in the seams of your clothing, or on your body?
key_questions.looking_for: Live lice or nits found in clothing seams, collars, cuffs, or waistbands

key_questions.question: When did the itching start, and has it been getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset days to weeks after infestation, slowly worsening; often present for weeks to months

key_questions.question: Does the itching get worse at night or when you wear or remove your clothes?
key_questions.looking_for: Continuous itching worse at night and with clothing use; relieved by bathing and washing clothes

key_questions.question: Have you had any sores, and are any of them painful, red, or draining?
key_questions.looking_for: Scratch marks and excoriations; purulence or spreading redness suggests secondary bacterial infection

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, severe headache, or body aches?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms suggesting a louse-borne illness such as typhus, trench fever, or relapsing fever

key_questions.question: Have you been able to bathe and wash your clothes and bedding regularly?
key_questions.looking_for: Limited access to showers, laundry, or clean clothing; poor hygiene is the main risk factor

key_questions.question: Where are you living right now — a shelter, encampment, or other crowded setting?
key_questions.looking_for: Crowded living conditions, homelessness, unstable housing, or recent displacement

key_questions.question: Has anyone close to you had similar itching or bugs in their clothing?
key_questions.looking_for: Close contacts or household members with the same infestation, supporting person-to-person spread

key_questions.question: Have you shared clothing, bedding, or towels with anyone who has been itching?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact with clothing, bedding, or towels used by an infested person

key_questions.question: Do you have pets at home, and have they been itchy or scratching?
key_questions.looking_for: Pets with fleas or mites; body lice do not come from animals, so this argues against a zoonotic cause

key_questions.question: Have you traveled recently to an area where sandflies or other vector-borne skin diseases are common?
key_questions.looking_for: Travel that would raise concern for leishmaniasis or another vector-borne skin disease

key_questions.question: Do you have any condition or take any medication that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunocompromising condition or immunosuppressive medication, which raises the risk of secondary infection and severe louse-borne disease

key_questions.question: Have you had any trouble sleeping or felt embarrassed or anxious about this?
key_questions.looking_for: Sleep disturbance and distress; also screen for delusional parasitosis if the belief of infestation is fixed despite negative exams

reasoning_points: Intense itching concentrated on the trunk, waist, groin, and upper thighs in areas covered by clothing
Live body lice or nits identified in the seams, collars, cuffs, or waistbands of the patient's clothing
Risk factors of poor hygiene, inability to launder clothing, crowded living conditions, or homelessness
Red bumps, excoriations, and scratch marks from bites and allergic reaction
Lice and nits absent from the scalp hair and pubic hair, distinguishing body lice from head lice and pubic lice
No burrows, tracks, or nodules in the finger webs, wrists, or genitalia, arguing against scabies
Fever, headache, or body aches considered as possible louse-borne illness such as typhus, trench fever, or relapsing fever
Secondary bacterial or fungal infection of scratch sores considered when there is purulence, spreading erythema, or fever

easy: Adult experiencing homelessness with intense itching under clothing
Visible lice and nits in the seams of the clothing on inspection
Excoriations and bite papules on the trunk, waist, and thighs
Clear history of inability to bathe or wash clothing regularly
medium: Patient reports itching and rash but does not mention bugs; lice and nits found only on careful inspection of clothing seams with a magnifying lens
Chronic infestation with thickened, darkened skin at the waist and groin and no obvious live lice
Scratch sores with early secondary bacterial infection
Itching attributed by the patient to dry skin or detergent
hard: Older adult with mild itching attributed to dry skin and no reported rash
Child with irritability and poor sleep who cannot describe the itching or report bugs in clothing
Immunocompromised patient with extensive secondary infection obscuring the underlying infestation
Patient with fever, headache, and body aches in whom a louse-borne illness such as typhus or relapsing fever must be recognized
Patient with a fixed belief of infestation but no lice or nits on repeated examination, raising concern for delusional parasitosis
